hints: Recall the order in Ala-Ser-Gly means Ala provides the free $\text{NH}_2$ end and Gly provides the free $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ end, with Ser in the middle.
Think about what side chain each residue carries (Ala has $\text{CH}_3$, Ser has $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, Gly has H) and how two $\text{CO-NH}$ links join them with loss of water.
walkthrough:
Get the three building blocks in the right order**
You are joining left to right as written: Ala then Ser then Gly. That means the left end keeps its amine, $\text{NH}_2$, and the right end keeps its carboxylic acid, $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. From the Data Booklet, Ala side chain is $\text{CH}_3$, Ser side chain is $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, Gly side chain is just H, so its alpha carbon is $\text{CH}_2$.

Join them with full peptide links**
A peptide bond forms when $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ of one amino acid condenses with $\text{NH}_2$ of the next, losing $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{NH}$. So draw $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{C}(=\text{O})$ linked to $\text{NHCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{C}(=\text{O})$ linked to $\text{NHCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Show every atom in the two $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{NH}$ groups, do not abbreviate to CONH.

Final answer: $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{NHCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{NHCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$
With both peptide bonds shown in full as $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{NH}$, free $\text{NH}_2$ at Ala end and free $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ at Gly end.

hints: Add the $M_r$ values of Ala, Ser and Gly, then remember that forming two peptide bonds removes two water molecules.
walkthrough:
Add then subtract water**
$ M_r(\text{Ala}) = 89 $, $ M_r(\text{Ser}) = 105 $, $ M_r(\text{Gly}) = 75 $. Sum $ = 89 + 105 + 75 = 269 $. Two condensations remove $ 2 \times 18 = 36 $. So $$M_r = 269 - 36 = 233$$ No units are needed for $M_r$.

hints: At pH 11, well above the isoelectric point, think about whether the $\text{NH}_3^+$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups will be protonated or deprotonated.
walkthrough:
Apply high pH to both ionisable groups**
Serine as a neutral molecule is $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, and as a zwitterion is $\text{NH}_3^+\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CO}_2^-$. At pH 11 the solution is strongly alkaline, so it removes protons. The carboxyl group stays as $\text{CO}_2^-$ and the ammonium group $\text{NH}_3^+$ is deprotonated to $\text{NH}_2$. The side chain $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is not ionised. So you get $$\text{NH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CO}_2^-$$ which is an anion with a single negative charge.

hints: Start with F at the top of the circuit, what must supply the electric field across the two electrodes?
Think about which side anions will move toward, and what that tells you about the polarity of G on the left where spots P to S have moved.
Consider what the strip labelled I that supports the spots must be soaked in to keep pH constant.
Match H to the electrode on the right hand side, opposite in polarity to G.
walkthrough:
F provides the field**
F is wired to both electrodes, so it must be the DC power supply that creates a constant potential difference.

G is where anions go**
At pH 11 all species are anions and the diagram shows them moving left from the origin toward G. Anions move to the positive electrode, so G is the anode, the positive electrode.

H is the opposite electrode**
H is on the right, connected to the other terminal of the supply, so it is the cathode, the negative electrode.

I is the support medium**
I is the strip on which the mixture is spotted and along which migration occurs. It is filter paper or gel soaked in buffer solution at pH 11 to maintain constant pH and allow ion movement.

Final answer: F: DC power supply
G: anode / positive electrode
H: cathode / negative electrode
I: filter paper (or gel) soaked in buffer solution

hints: At pH 11 all four species are singly charged anions, so charge is the same and only another property controls how far they move.
Compare the $M_r$ values: glycine is about 75 while the tripeptide is 233, so think about which experiences more friction through the paper.
Look at the diagram: P has moved furthest toward the anode G, while S has barely moved from the origin, so assign smallest to P and largest to S.
walkthrough:
Fix the charge first**
At pH 11, Ala, Ser, Gly and Ala-Ser-Gly all exist mainly as $1-$ anions ($\text{NH}_2...\text{CO}_2^-$). So they are all attracted to the positive electrode G on the left. Charge does not separate them here.

Let size decide the race**
With equal charge, the smaller the ion the less resistance from the paper or gel and the faster it migrates. Glycine, $M_r = 75$, is the smallest of the four. The tripeptide, $M_r = 233$, is by far the largest.

Read P and S from the plate**
P is closest to G, it has travelled furthest, so it must be the fastest, smallest species: glycine, $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2^-$. S is closest to the origin, it has hardly moved, so it must be the slowest, largest species: the tripeptide anion $[\text{Ala-Ser-Gly}]^-$.

Final answer: Spot P: glycine, $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2^-$ (or $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ as neutral formula)
Spot S: tripeptide anion, $[\text{Ala-Ser-Gly}]^-$
Explanation: at pH 11 all are anions with similar charge, so mobility depends on size; glycine is smallest so moves fastest/furthest to anode; tripeptide is largest so moves slowest/least.

hints: Breaking peptide amide links back to free amino acids needs aqueous acid or alkali plus heating, not just water at room temperature.
walkthrough:
Choose a harsh aqueous reagent**
Peptide bonds are stable amides. To split them you boil the tripeptide with dilute hydrochloric acid, often written as heat with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, or boil with aqueous sodium hydroxide, $\text{OH}^-\text{(aq)}$. Heating is essential to break the $\text{C-N}$ links and release the three free amino acids.
Final answer: Heat with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ / dilute $\text{HCl(aq)}$ / $\text{H}^+\text{(aq)}$ OR heat with $\text{OH}^-\text{(aq)}$ / $\text{NaOH(aq)}$

hints: The peptide bonds are split by adding water across the $\text{C-N}$ bond, so name the reaction type that uses water to break a bond.
walkthrough:
Name the water splitting process**
Each $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{NH}$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ gives $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ plus $\text{NH}_2$. Because water is used to break the bonds, the reaction type is hydrolysis.
